Human evolution. The process by which anatomically and behaviorally modern humans emerged from non-human primate ancestors over millions of years. This process involved gradual changes in body structure, brain development, tool use, and social complexity, shaped by environmental pressures and natural selection.

The human lineage diverged from other African apes around six to seven million years ago. A defining moment was the emergence of bipedalism—walking upright on two legs. This freed hands for tool-making and carrying food. Australopithecus lived four to two million years ago. They were early bipedal hominins with small brains of four hundred to five hundred cubic centimeters. They may have used simple tools but lacked language and complex culture. Their fossils show pronounced sexual dimorphism. Homo erectus lived two million to one hundred thousand years ago and showed dramatic increases in brain size of seven hundred to twelve hundred cubic centimeters. They controlled fire use and made more sophisticated stone tools called hand axes. Homo erectus were the first hominins to leave Africa and colonize Eurasia.

Homo sapiens, our species, emerged in Africa around three hundred thousand years ago. By seventy thousand years ago, behavioural modernity appeared with symbolic thinking, language, art, and ritualized burial. This great leap may reflect a genetic mutation affecting language capacity. The Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania is a key archaeological site where early stone tools and hominin fossils reveal the transition to tool-making and hunting. Tool-making, hunting, language, and social cooperation—hallmarks of human culture—evolved gradually and are linked to brain expansion driven by natural selection.

The Paleolithic era represents the vast period when human ancestors lived by hunting and gathering, the lifestyle for over ninety-nine percent of human history. Humans remained in Africa until Homo sapiens dispersed globally around seventy thousand years ago. Language likely emerged gradually over millions of years as brain size increased and social structures grew more complex. It enabled abstract thought, planning, and cultural transmission. Comparison with other primates reveals capacities that are uniquely human: abstract symbolic thought, recursive grammar, theory of mind, and capacity for cumulative culture.
